questions.q: What does the acronym 'PENTA' stand for in the National Immunisation Schedule, and at which three ages is it administered?
questions.a: PENTA stands for a combination vaccine containing DPT (Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus), Hepatitis B, and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b). It is administered at 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks. A wrong answer (e.g., "PENTA is only DPT" or "given at birth") reveals the student has not memorised the schedule components or confuses PENTA with the birth dose of Hepatitis B.

questions.q: Why is the BCG vaccine given at birth while the Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine is delayed until 9 months?
questions.a: BCG is given at birth because tuberculosis exposure can occur immediately and the newborn's immune system can respond to this live attenuated vaccine despite maternal antibodies. MR is delayed until 9 months because high levels of maternal anti-measles antibodies (transferred via placenta) neutralise the live vaccine virus if given earlier, preventing seroconversion. A wrong answer (e.g., "BCG is stronger" or "MR is for older children") shows misunderstanding of maternal antibody interference with live vaccines.

questions.q: A 14-week-old infant has received BCG, OPV (birth), Hepatitis B (birth), and two doses of PENTA (at 6 and 10 weeks). Which vaccines are due at the 14-week visit, and what is the minimum interval from the previous PENTA dose?
questions.a: At 14 weeks, the infant is due for the third dose of PENTA and the third dose of OPV. The minimum interval between PENTA doses is 4 weeks (28 days). A wrong answer (e.g., "only OPV" or "MR vaccine") indicates the student cannot track the multi-dose series or confuses the 14-week visit with the 9-month visit.

questions.q: Compare the immune response to a live attenuated vaccine (e.g., OPV) versus an inactivated vaccine (e.g., Hepatitis B). How does this difference influence the number of doses required in the schedule?
questions.a: Live attenuated vaccines (OPV) replicate mildly in the host, mimicking natural infection and stimulating robust, long-lasting humoral and cellular immunity with fewer doses (e.g., 3 primary doses + boosters). Inactivated/subunit vaccines (Hep B) cannot replicate; they require multiple doses (3 primary doses) to achieve protective antibody titers and often need boosters because antibody levels wane faster. A wrong answer (e.g., "both need same doses" or "live vaccines need more doses") shows failure to link vaccine type to immunological memory generation.

questions.q: A parent argues: "Polio has been eradicated in India, so the OPV doses in the schedule are unnecessary and only cause side effects." Critique this argument using epidemiological principles.
questions.a: The argument is flawed. Eradication in India (certified 2014) does not mean global eradication; wild poliovirus persists in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Importation risk remains high due to travel/migration. Herd immunity must be maintained (OPV coverage >80%) to prevent outbreaks if the virus is imported. Additionally, OPV provides intestinal mucosal immunity (IgA) that reduces transmission – a benefit IPV alone does not fully give. Stopping OPV prematurely would create an immunity gap. A wrong answer (e.g., "polio is gone so stop") reveals confusion between elimination (local) and eradication (global) and ignorance of herd immunity thresholds.

questions.q: Design a simplified immunisation reminder card for a low-literacy rural mother. Show vaccines due at each visit (birth, 6w, 10w, 14w, 9m, 15m, 16-24m, 2y, 5y, 10y, 16y) using only symbols/pictures. Explain your design choices for two specific vaccines.
questions.a: A good answer includes: a timeline with icons (syringe, calendar, sun/moon for age), colour-coded visits, and pictograms for each vaccine (e.g., lung for BCG, drops for OPV, shield for PENTA, measles rash for MR). For BCG: use a shield with "TB" crossed out, given at birth (newborn icon). For MR: use a spotted face (measles) and a pregnant woman with a crossed-out rubella virus, given at 9 months (baby sitting icon). Poor answer: text-heavy, no visual hierarchy, or incorrect ages (e.g., MR at birth). Reveals inability to translate technical schedule into accessible health communication.
